findings.where: First screen, the row of five outlined pills (PPP Law, Infrastructure, Development banks, Governments, Risk allocation) just above the email action
findings.fault: The pills are drawn like buttons or filters, but none of them does anything. They sit right above the one action, so the screen seems to offer six things to click instead of one. They also only repeat words from the lead sentence above them as labels, and add no evidence.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer who taps 'PPP Law' or 'Development banks' expecting his work on that theme, gets nothing, and has to look again for the real way in. Mark, whose one action now competes with five dead controls.

findings.where: First screen, the claim 'I advise multilateral development banks, development agencies and governments…' and the area around the action
findings.fault: The hero states who Mark serves but gives nothing a reader can check: no named body that asked for his work, no region or country where he has worked, no recent talk or article with its venue. The only things near the action are the claim and the topic pills. Per first-visit trust, a visitor must be sure he has done this work for bodies like theirs, in their region (items 3, 6, 14; 'Feel the CV').
findings.who_objects: A procurement-minded officer arriving from LinkedIn who selects consultants against terms of reference. 'I advise development banks' is something anyone can write. Without one checkable specific, they have no reason to write instead of comparing other consultants.

findings.where: Phone, the first screen (top 844 px of phone-01)
findings.fault: On a phone the portrait comes first and fills most of the first screen. A visitor sees the nav, the photo and only the start of the heading. The sentence saying what Mark does and for whom, and the email address, are a full screen further down. So the 5-second test fails at phone width: a face and an opinion, with no offer and no way to reach him.
findings.who_objects: An officer opening the link from LinkedIn on a phone (the most likely way to arrive). They see a man's photo and 'In my view, we are at a turning point…' with no sign of what he offers or how to get in touch, unless they scroll.

findings.where: First screen, the heading 'In my view, we are at a turning point in the story of public-private partnerships.'
findings.fault: The heading promises an argument: what the turning point is. Nothing on the page delivers it or links to the post it comes from (Blog No. 2, 2020). The specimen article below is a different post, and the newest-work slot is a different lecture. The visitor is left with a claim and nowhere to follow it.
findings.who_objects: A reader intrigued by the line who wants to judge Mark's thinking: the strongest hook on the page leads nowhere. Mark, whose opinion is shown without the reasoning that makes it credible.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the byline and the end of the article (after the lecture PDF link)
findings.fault: An article a LinkedIn post links to gives only 'Mark Moseley · MMM Infra Blog No. 8 · date'. There is no one-line bio saying who he is or what he advises on, and no email address at the end. A reader who lands deep on an article cannot tell who wrote it or how to reach him (first-visit trust items 7 and 12).
findings.who_objects: An officer who arrives on an article from a shared post, is persuaded by the argument, and finds no route to the author without going looking for the homepage. The articles are the product, so this is where many first visits start.

findings.where: First screen as a whole: the diagonal hatching over the blue field, the outsized ghost 'PPP' behind the heading, the pill tags and the white button with an arrow
findings.fault: Together these read as a software product's landing page, not a senior legal advisor's page. Pill tags, a hatched brand field and a button with an arrow are the stock kit any consultancy or start-up could own. This works against the brief's 'refined', 'nothing in-your-face techy' and 'a look any consultancy could own'.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the founder, who asked that the page reflect law and advice to governments and pass the personal-advisor test. A government or bank reader may also take the polish as salesy, which the research names as a failure ('slick, salesy').
